analysis.title: GREED & fear - Tech Cold War
key_insights: Markets are behaving as if AI capex has peaked despite no compelling on-the-ground evidence. Wood's open question is whether this is a cycle peak or a mid-cycle correction.

Nvidia has acted as the banker of AI: US$42bn in buyouts, US$61bn in equity stakes across 229 startups and 13 public companies, and US$164.5bn in lease guarantees and cloud capacity backstops, alongside US$63.1bn of customer receivables with terms up to a year (per Tunguz).
Interim CEO Colette Kress reportedly had reservations about Huang's deal-making exposure. A more conservative Nvidia would tighten funding across the AI ecosystem, especially neoclouds.

CoreWeave shares are down 25% since the Huang story broke and its bonds yield 15.7%, which Wood calls starting to look existential. Loss of speculative compute demand could lower compute prices for others.
The Huang affair has reactivated US national security hawks. Democrats take Congress on 3 January, so legislative pressure on chip exports to China is set to rise (Chip Security Act, Match Act).
Jefferies' Edison Lee estimates up to 240,000 Nvidia AI chips were diverted to China since 2024. IFP estimates Megaspeed rents about 86,000 GPUs to Alibaba and other Chinese customers.
BIS now requires export licences for AI chips to Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Singapore and Brazil unless the buyer is a US company. The aim is to stop Chinese access through offshore leasing.

Escalating US political noise raises the risk of Chinese stock sanctions or MSCI removal, and China 'uninvestable' talk could return, especially if the next president is from the national security faction. Trump is seen as the best US president China could hope for.

China is pushing self-reliance. YMTC plans to source up to 70% of equipment domestically for its fourth Wuhan fab. Wood's base case is that the US has lost the chips-for-rare-earths trade, and the Busan truce expires 10 January.
Hyperscaler 'other non-operating income' swung from +US$155bn in 2Q26 to -US$9bn in 3Q26. Annualised net income is up 73% over six quarters, but excluding that item it is up only 15%.
The 10-year Treasury yield is 5.1% despite risk-off and a 12% post-midterm oil decline, so there is no safe-haven bid at the long end.

US fiscal deterioration: net interest plus entitlements are 98.4% of receipts, FY26 deficit US$1.99tn (6.2% of GDP), and net interest a record US$1.064tn. Wood's base case is eventual financial repression, and the debt limit is expected to bind in February or March.
Malaysia has 61 data center projects announced since 2023 with 8.35GW maximum demand, against 42GW installed capacity.

Thailand's private investment is booming: real private GFCF +16.2% YoY in 3Q26 and BOI-approved FDI Bt1.29tn in 9M26 (+64% YoY), with 66% in digital. Singapore-sourced FDI is likely China-linked, with limited domestic multipliers.
Thai macro: government debt 68.3% of GDP versus a 70% soft ceiling, and the current account surplus has fallen to 0.2% of GDP. The baht has stayed stable despite a 1.0% policy rate.
Asean FDI hit a record US$244bn in 2025 but is only 2.7% of MSCI EM. Chip smuggling scrutiny makes the region's neutrality harder to maintain.

Gold broke US$3,800/oz, Wood's hoped-for bottom of the range, so the moment of truth is at hand. China's official reserves rose 25.82 tonnes in October (24th straight monthly rise) and central banks bought a net 321.2 tonnes last quarter.
Portfolio change: Asia Pacific ex-Japan overweight India raised by 1ppt to 15%, Taiwan cut by 1ppt to 23%.

market_movers.rationale: Shares are 27% below the pre-Busan level. The Huang affair, tighter export controls and a possibly more conservative financing stance are headwinds.
Shares are down 25% since the story broke and bonds yield 15.7%, reflecting dependence on Nvidia funding.

sector_views.rationale: Nvidia funding tightening and export restrictions threaten speculative compute demand.
Large investment pipelines in Malaysia and Thailand, but new US remote access restrictions create risk.

earnings_insights: Four US hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta) reported 'other non-operating income' of -US$9bn in 3Q26 versus +US$155bn in 2Q26.

Hyperscaler annualised combined net income was US$588bn in the 12 months to 3Q26, versus US$340bn in the 12 months to 1Q25. Annualised other non-operating income is US$209bn (from US$12bn) and the remainder US$379bn (from US$329bn).

macro_indicators.interpretation: No safe-haven bid despite equity risk-off.
Oil weakness has not pulled long yields down.
Fiscal deterioration supports Wood's financial repression base case.
Ultra-low rates with a stable baht.
Surplus has largely vanished, removing a baht support.
Breaks the range bottom Wood hoped would hold.

trade_ideas.description: Asia Pacific ex-Japan relative-return portfolio: raise India weight by 1ppt to 15%, cut Taiwan by 1ppt to 23%
trade_ideas.rationale: Portfolio adjustment amid AI and Nvidia-related risk, as stated in the report.

risk_factors: Peak in AI capex and tighter Nvidia financing of neoclouds.
Escalating US export controls and Chinese stock sanction or MSCI exclusion risk.
US fiscal deterioration, a 5.1% 10-year yield and the debt ceiling in February or March.
Gold failing to hold the US$3,800 level.

tension_points.bull_case: No compelling on-the-ground evidence yet that AI capex has peaked, so the market sell-off may be a mid-cycle correction.
tension_points.bear_case: Markets and Wood's own prior note argue for a peak. Nvidia financing may tighten, CoreWeave bonds yield 15.7%, and hyperscaler profits relied on non-operating gains.

theme_stances.evidence: any move to a more conservative approach will have tightening implications
